cues.text: A Greek Physician of Antioch
Luke , by strong and ancient tradition a native of Antioch in Syria, appears to have been a Gentile convert to the faith.

Traditionally regarded as the only New Testament writer who was not Jewish, he was a physician by profession, a detail St. Paul himself confirms, addressing him in one epistle as "Luke the beloved physician."
Unlike the Apostles, Luke was almost certainly not an eyewitness to the events of Christ's earthly ministry; he tells us so himself in the careful opening lines of his Gospel.

He explains that he has undertaken to compile an orderly account only after diligently investigating everything from eyewitness testimony passed down to him — the meticulous method of a trained mind accustomed to careful observation.
A Companion on the Road
Luke first enters the narrative of Acts at Troas, where the account shifts abruptly into the first person plural: “we sought to go on into Macedonia.”
This subtle but unmistakable sign indicates that the author had personally joined Paul's missionary band at that very point.
From Troas onward, Luke's presence recurs throughout Acts wherever this same "we" reappears: crossing into Europe and journeying to Jerusalem.
He remained with Paul through the long, dangerous sea voyage and shipwreck that carried the Apostle finally to Rome.
He was a companion who did not merely record Paul's missionary journeys from a distance, but walked, sailed, and suffered through a considerable portion of them himself.
The Gospel of Mercy
Luke's own Gospel reflects, more than any other, a particular tenderness toward those the ancient world was most inclined to overlook.

It alone preserves the Nativity narrative as it likely came from Mary's own remembered testimony, the parables of the Prodigal Son and the Good Samaritan, and sustained attention to women, the poor, tax collectors and sinners, and the marginalized.
This attention has led the whole Christian tradition to call it, above the other three, the Gospel of Mercy .
A later, cherished tradition — impossible now to verify but treasured nonetheless — holds that Luke was also a painter.
It holds that he made the very first portrait of the Blessed Virgin Mary.

Whether or not the tradition is literally true, it captures something genuine about a Gospel whose written portrait of Mary and of Christ's own mercy remains, in its own way, among the most vivid ever composed.
A Second Book for the Church
Luke did not stop with the story of Christ's earthly life; his second volume, the Acts of the Apostles , continues the narrative into the life of the young Church.
It traces the Gospel's spread from Jerusalem to Rome itself and preserves our only sustained historical account of the Apostolic age.
The whole Church owes this debt to one careful physician's determination that this unfolding story, too, deserved to be set down accurately for those who would come after.
Present to the End
Luke's faithfulness to Paul did not waver even as the Apostle's own life drew toward its close.
In his final letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution, Paul laments that several companions have deserted him or been sent elsewhere.
He adds, with evident and simple gratitude: "only Luke is with me."
Of all the friends and fellow workers accompanying Paul across decades of missionary labor, Luke was named as remaining with him during his final imprisonment.
Legacy
Tradition holds that Luke, unmarried and remarkably long-lived for the ancient world, died in Greece, variously placed in Boeotia or Achaia.
He was around eighty-four, with the later tradition placing his death after the deaths of many of the first missionary generation.
Patron of physicians, surgeons, and artists, Luke is represented in Christian art by the winged ox, a symbol drawn from his Gospel's opening scene in the Temple.
He remains a model of the careful, humble scholarship that the Church has always needed alongside its more dramatic witnesses.
His example proves that a physician's patient attention to evidence and a friend's quiet, unwavering loyalty can, together, leave behind two of the most treasured books the New Testament possesses.
